title: Poolside Resort Kitchen Planner
description: Users design a luxury resort poolside bar area by positioning commercial refrigerators around a central pool. The planner enforces a total energy budget across all placed refrigerators, couples refrigerator proximity to the pool with a cooling-efficiency modifier, and supports full undo/redo of every placement, rotation, and deletion action.
prompt: Create a single HTML file using Three.js r170 that implements a poolside resort kitchen layout planner. Load pool.glb centered at the origin as the fixed anchor of the scene, scaled so it occupies roughly 8x4 world units. Load CommercialRefrigerator.glb as a clonable asset the user can stamp into the scene. Set up a perspective camera at elevation 12 units looking down at 45 degrees with OrbitControls for rotation and zoom. Add ambient light intensity 0.6 plus a directional sun light casting soft shadows. Render on a ground plane textured as stone tile. Implement these interactions: (1) Click an Add Refrigerator button to spawn a new unit at a default position; each unit draws from a shared 100-kW energy budget displayed in a top HUD bar. (2) Click-drag any refrigerator to reposition it on the ground plane using raycasting; snapping to a 0.5-unit grid. (3) Right-click a refrigerator to rotate it 90 degrees. (4) Double-click to delete a refrigerator, returning its energy to the budget. (5) Proximity rule: refrigerators within 2 units of the pool edge get a 1.5x cooling-efficiency bonus shown as a green glow outline; farther units show orange. (6) Each refrigerator consumes 15 kW base, but efficiency-boosted ones consume only 10 kW, dynamically updating the budget. (7) Implement an undo/redo stack (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) that records every add, move, rotate, and delete action and fully restores prior state including positions, rotations, and energy totals. (8) A summary panel shows count of placed units, total consumption, remaining budget, and number of efficiency-boosted units. Prevent adding a refrigerator if the budget would be exceeded. Use at least 10 interaction steps in a typical workflow: add 4 units, drag each near the pool, rotate 2, delete 1, undo the delete, redo it, then add another. All state must remain consistent through undo/redo cycles.
